historical_record.description: The Music Concourse, of almost nine acres, was completed as the Grand Court of Honor for the California Mid-Winter International Exposition, which opened in January 1894.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 96: the Francis Scott Key Monument, at the northeast end of the concourse.

The sculptor William W. Story was contracted to make the Francis Scott Key Monument, paid for from James Lick's bequest — the first monument to Key in the United States. It was made in Italy and arrived from Genoa on 25 January 1888 after a 187-day voyage.
The Key Monument was dedicated before some 60,000 people with "The Star-Spangled Banner" and a 100-gun salute.
Damaged in the 1906 earthquake, the Key Monument was repaired for $9,000 in 1909 and moved to the side of the present concourse.

The Key Monument was taken down and stored in the park's corporation yard to clear room for a new California Academy of Sciences building; it was later restored, for about $130,000, by Reginald Locke and Associates.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 249, Music Concourse.

At the suggestion of the attorney Joseph D. Redding, the Park Commission began rebuilding the Midwinter Fair's Grand Court of Honor as a Music Concourse, to a plan largely following an unnamed surveyor's circulation scheme; the bowl had been excavated for the fair under M. M. O'Shaughnessy. A statue of Ulysses S. Grant was added the same year.
The Goethe and Schiller Monument was set up in front of the de Young Museum.
The statue of Thomas Starr King, placed in the Rhododendron Dell in 1892, was moved to the concourse.
The Lion statue was set up.
The Sundial and the Padre Junípero Serra Monument were set up.
The Giuseppe Verdi Monument and the Charles Hall Page fountains were set up.
The bust of Ludwig van Beethoven was set up.
The Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra group was set up.
The Robert Emmet statue was set up.
The General John Joseph Pershing Monument was set up.
The Corinne Rideout Fountain was set up.
The Phoebe Apperson Hearst Memorial Fountain was set up, where one of the concourse's 1896 staircases had been.
The Sphinxes, the last of the concourse's contributing monuments, were set up; its layout has been unchanged since. The monuments added after 1900 were probably placed by John McLaren.

The United Railroads, which like the Market Street Railway before it had paid the Park Band to draw riders to the park, ended its support; the Park Commission grudgingly funded a thirty-piece band under Charles Cassassa, later led by Ralph Murray and Alfred Arriola, and from 1973 by Col. Robert Hansen as the Municipal Band.
